Introducing the Journal of AI Generated Papers (JAIGP)
AI can now write papers.
But journals were never designed for that.
Over the past few years, academic publishing has been grappling with AI systems that are increasingly capable of writing, analyzing data, and even outlining full research projects. The dominant response so far has been defensive, focused on detection and disclosure.
But what if we approached this differently?
What if AI-generated papers, or AIGPs, had their own outlet?
Today, we (Claud and I) are introducing JAIGP: the Journal of AI Generated Papers (jaigp.org), a multidisciplinary journal dedicated explicitly to papers generated by AI systems.
At JAIGP, AIs are authors and humans act as prompters.
But before you decide whether you love or hate this idea, let me explain why we built it, and how we’re trying to make it work.
Let’s start with why
Scientific journals are social technologies that define norms around authorship, credit, and credibility. Trying to squeeze AIGPs into these journals is complicated. It creates ambiguity for readers, reviewers, and editors alike. By creating a venue dedicated to AIGPs, we can make the distinction explicit and honest.
JAIGP is not about replacing traditional scholarship, but about building a transparent ecosystem where this new form of knowledge production can be explored on its own terms.
Every paper in JAIGP is an experiment in human-AI collaboration. Some will be insightful, others speculative, and many may not be very good, and this is precisely the point. Our guiding principle is learning through collaborative exploration.
We designed JAIGP as a lightweight institutional experiment, with features intended to make this new space more transparent, exploratory, and legible.
But even experimental spaces need some rules and guardrails.
So we introduced a few simple mechanisms to keep the platform open while discouraging low-effort noise:
ORCID authentication ensures contributors have verified scholarly identities.
A publication badge system (Gold, Silver, Copper, New), based on verified non-AIGP publications, provides a lightweight signal of prompter experience and helps readers contextualize contributions.
Papers can only be updated once per hour, encouraging meaningful iteration rather than rapid micro-edits.These are not prestige markers, but transparency tools meant to help readers quickly understand who is behind a prompt.
How to contribute?

There are essentially two ways to create AIGPs.
The slow way is to use web-based AI interfaces like ChatGPT, Perplexity, or Gemini.
The supercharged way is to use command-line AI tools like Claude. The difference is profound: command-line tools can interact directly with a file system, download data, install packages, and write code locally. Instead of copying and pasting from a browser, the AI can reshape datasets, run models, generate figures, and compile papers directly on your machine.
The workflow and throughput of this is orders of magnitude higher than that of web interfaces and are the preferred choice of people exploring AIGPs.
To conclude.
AI is not just a tool. It is a technology that is reshaping the boundary between thinking, writing, and discovery.
We can pretend this shift isn’t happening, or we can build institutions that help us study it in the open.
JAIGP is a small step in that direction: an attempt to make machine authorship legible and to build a clearer taxonomy of knowledge production in the age of AI.
